name: Hyaluronic acid filler

lead: Hyaluronic acid fillers are injectable gels used to add volume and smooth folds in the lips, cheeks and lines around the mouth. They are the most widely used type of dermal filler, and randomized trials and meta-analyses support their effect on volume and wrinkles.
Results are temporary, commonly lasting around six months or longer depending on product and area, and the gel can be dissolved with an enzyme if the result is unwanted.

paras: The gel physically fills space and binds water, and some studies report that it also prompts nearby skin cells to make new collagen.

Most side effects are short-lived swelling, redness and bruising. Rare but serious complications include blocked blood vessels causing tissue death and, in the worst cases, permanent vision loss; guidelines describe emergency treatment with hyaluronidase. In the US fillers are regulated as medical devices and injected by licensed providers.

lead: Hyaluronic acid (HA) fillers are injectable gels, most often based on cross-linked hyaluronic acid, placed under the skin to restore volume, soften folds and wrinkles, and reshape areas such as the lips, cheeks and nasolabial folds. Hyaluronic acid is a naturally occurring component of skin, and reviews describe HA gels as the most commonly used dermal filler [1]. Well-known product lines include Juvederm and Restylane.

Clinicians describe HA fillers as temporary and reversible: the gel can be dissolved with the enzyme hyaluronidase, and the effect may last longer than the physical persistence of the gel because of possible collagen stimulation [1][2]. Randomized trials and systematic reviews report that most side effects are short-lived injection-site reactions such as swelling and bruising, while rare complications, including vascular occlusion and vision loss, can be serious and in some cases permanent [3][4][5].

In looksmaxxing discussions the procedure appears mainly as a non-surgical option for lips, cheeks, chin and under-eye hollows, usually discussed alongside surgery and fat grafting. The published evidence on its effect on facial attractiveness specifically is limited to a small number of studies, while evidence for volume and wrinkle correction is more extensive [6][7].

paras: HA fillers are sterile gels of hyaluronic acid, a sugar-based polymer found in skin and connective tissue that binds water [1][8]. Products differ in how heavily the HA is cross-linked, in particle size and in stiffness, and these physical properties influence how a gel behaves in different facial areas [8]. Most commercial HA fillers use a chemical cross-linker, commonly BDDE, to make the gel last longer in tissue [9].

Reviews describe the gel as working by filling and volumizing, and also by attracting water to the injected area [1]. Some research has reported that cross-linked HA injected into photodamaged skin was followed by new collagen production, which may partly explain why effects can outlast the gel itself [10][1].

Reported uses include correcting nasolabial folds, augmenting the lips, restoring midface volume and softening fine perioral lines [4][6]. A related use is the so-called skin booster, in which low-concentration HA products are placed in the dermis for hydration rather than volume; one review of the concept has since been retracted by its journal [11].
Clinicians also use HA to alter facial contour, for example in cheek augmentation, which one clinical trial linked to improved self-rated feelings of facial attractiveness [7].

A meta-analysis of lip augmentation studies, covering 32 records in its descriptive review and 10 in its quantitative synthesis, concluded that HA is an effective lip filler [6]. A split-face comparison of fillers has examined collagen and elastin stimulation after HA injection versus calcium hydroxylapatite [12], and a controlled trial reported collagen production in photodamaged skin after cross-linked HA injection [10].

Trials also compare HA with other products or combinations, such as a randomized study of botulinum toxin combined with a skin-booster HA product for periorbital wrinkles [13]. Duration varies by product, site and individual; general overviews describe effects commonly lasting about six months to longer, with repeat treatment needed to maintain results [9].

Controlled human research includes a meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials on adverse events [4], a systematic review of 48 randomized studies on safety [3], a meta-analysis of lip augmentation [6], a randomized split-face histology study comparing HA with calcium hydroxylapatite [12], a controlled trial of collagen production in photodamaged skin [10] and a trial of cheek augmentation and self-rated attractiveness [7]. ClinicalTrials.gov also lists registered studies of HA fillers for midface volume, lip appearance and comparisons between HA products.

A systematic review of 48 high-level-evidence randomized studies grouped adverse events into expected reactions, product- or technique-related events and severe events, and found that most were short-lived injection-site reactions that resolved on their own within weeks [3]. A meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials examined adverse-event rates by facial location, comparing the nasolabial fold with the midface, perioral and lip regions [4].

Rare complications include vascular occlusion, in which filler blocks or travels through a blood vessel, leading to tissue necrosis or, if it reaches the eye's blood supply, vision loss, which review authors describe as often irreversible [5][14][15]. Delayed nodules, infection and hypersensitivity reactions have also been described [15][2].

Published guidance recommends prompt recognition and treatment of occlusion, including high-dose hyaluronidase protocols, although controlled data are limited and recommendations differ between expert groups [14][16][2][17].

HA fillers are not pharmacologically active in the usual sense. Reviews describe them as biodegradable, with a negligible risk of immune or allergic reaction compared with some other fillers, and rapidly degraded by hyaluronidase [1][8].

In the United States dermal fillers are regulated as medical devices and are injected by licensed providers; in the UK and European Economic Area they require a CE mark, which certifies manufacturing standards rather than clinical efficacy [9]. Dermal fillers are described as among the most popular cosmetic procedures [4].

lore.intro: HA filler is discussed in appearance communities as the standard reversible, non-surgical injectable, often compared with surgery for lips, cheeks and chin.
